concept.name: Regime-switching model
concept.definition: A time-series model in which the parameters change according to a latent discrete state that itself follows a Markov chain, so the series alternates between distinct regimes such as low-volatility expansion and high-volatility contraction. Hamilton (1989) introduced the framework for business-cycle dynamics.
concept.intuition: The market behaves like two different machines, calm and stormy, and an invisible switch flips between them; at any moment you only have a probability of which machine is running.
concept.mechanics: An unobserved state s_t in {1,...,N} follows a first-order Markov chain with transition probabilities p_ij, and conditional on s_t the observation follows a regime-specific process (e.g., different means and variances). The Hamilton filter computes filtered regime probabilities recursively, parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, and smoothed probabilities give retrospective regime dating.
concept.formula: y_t | s_t ~ f(y_t; theta_{s_t}) with P(s_t = j | s_{t-1} = i) = p_ij; e.g., y_t = mu_{s_t} + phi (y_{t-1} - mu_{s_{t-1}}) + sigma_{s_t} epsilon_t.
concept.failure_modes: Regimes are unidentified unless the sample contains enough transitions, and the likelihood is multimodal with label-switching issues. The model assumes abrupt switches, so slowly evolving parameters are forced into spurious extra regimes or poor fits.
concept.misconceptions: That filtered regime probabilities are certain knowledge of the current state: they are model-conditional probabilities, and small misspecifications can flip the inferred regime.
concept.example: Hamilton modeled U.S. GNP growth with two regimes, positive-growth expansion and negative-growth contraction, whose filtered probabilities closely track NBER recession dates.
